Volume 13 · Chapter 06

Static games and refinements

Graduate Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v13-c05

By the endEstablish strategic equilibria and analyze equilibrium selection.

Volume 13 · Chapter 6

Static games and refinements

A recommendation to wait can be optimal when it reveals that somebody else will act, yet unattractive before that information arrives. An action can be a best reply to a perfectly precise forecast but fail against every fully mixed perturbation. Equilibrium analysis must specify both beliefs and the deviations that a player can make. Those choices distinguish Nash, Bayesian, perfect, correlated and coarse correlated equilibrium.

Capability. Prove finite mixed Nash and Bayesian existence; characterize strategic-form trembling-hand perfection in two equivalent ways; solve complete equilibrium correspondences in original small games; and derive exactly what private recommendations and different deviation rights imply. Six worked cases and twelve solved exercises separate existence, selection, welfare and empirical prediction.

Prerequisites. Uncertainty and information supplies expected utility and conditional beliefs. The complete finite-dimensional Kakutani proof in General equilibrium and existence supplies our fixed-point theorem, with no circular appeal to Nash. Welfare, aggregation and social choice distinguishes individual utility from a declared social objective. Elementary strategic interaction appears in Game theory; this chapter supplies the retained finite mixed-existence proof.

1. Finite strategies, support and mixed Nash existence

A finite strategic-form game has players i=1,…,n, finite nonempty action sets Ai, and payoff functions ui:A→ℝ on A=∏iAi. Payoffs are von Neumann–Morgenstern utility indices. If a table is interpreted as money, its expected-payoff calculations assume risk neutrality over those amounts. The games below are synthetic; their numbers are not estimated behavior or promised returns.

A mixed strategy σi∈Δ(Ai) assigns nonnegative probabilities summing to one. Its support is {ai:σi(ai)>0}; it is fully mixed when every action has positive probability. A mixed-strategy profile means independent randomization across players. Thus

Ui(σ)=Σa∈Aui(a)∏jσj(aj),
vi(ai,σ−i)=Σa−iui(ai,a−i)∏j≠iσj(aj),
Ui(σ)=Σaiσi(ai)vi(ai,σ−i).

The finite polynomial Ui is continuous and linear in each player’s own probabilities, holding the others fixed. It is not generally jointly linear in the profile. A joint distribution μ∈Δ(A), allowing correlation, is a different object from a list of independent marginal strategies.

Support criterion. Against fixed σ−i, a mixture is a best reply if and only if every supported action attains maxbivi(bi,σ−i). The expected payoff is a convex average of the finitely many pure-action payoffs. It equals their maximum exactly when it places no positive weight on a strictly smaller value. Consequently checking all pure unilateral deviations is equivalent to checking every mixed unilateral deviation. Indifference among supported actions alone is insufficient unless excluded actions are no better.

A Nash equilibrium is σ with Ui(σ)≥vi(bi,σ−i) for every i and bi. The player changes only its own strategy, and opponents retain their strategies. This is a consistency and incentive condition, not a theorem about how beliefs were acquired or how play converges.

Finite mixed Nash theorem and proof. Let X=∏iΔ(Ai), a nonempty compact convex subset of a finite-dimensional Euclidean space. Define Bi(σ)=argmaxρi∈Δ(Ai)Ui(ρi,σ−i). A highest-payoff pure action exists, so Bi is nonempty. By the support criterion it is the simplex on the maximizing actions, hence compact and convex. Its graph is closed: if σk→σ and ρik→ρi with ρik∈Bi(σk), then for every pure bi,

Ui(ρik,σ−ik)≥vi(bi,σ−ik).

Continuity passes each inequality to the limit; the support criterion makes ρi a best reply. The product correspondence B=∏Bi has nonempty compact convex values and a closed graph in X×X. The finite-dimensional Kakutani theorem proved in Chapter 4 gives σ∈B(σ), precisely a Nash equilibrium. This proves existence in every finite game, including games without a pure equilibrium. It does not prove uniqueness, efficient play or convergence of repeated best replies.

Worked case 1: a unique mixed equilibrium with a saddle certificate

The row player chooses U or D and the column player L or R. The row payoff matrix is ((3,−1),(−2,2)); column payoff is its negative. Write p=Pr(U), q=Pr(L). Against q the row payoffs are 4q−1 and 2−4q. Against p the expected row payoffs in columns L and R are 5p−2 and 2−3p; the column player minimizes these.

There is no pure saddle: row best replies are U to L and D to R, while column best replies are R to U and L to D. If one player were pure in an equilibrium, the other’s strict best reply would be pure, contradicting the absence of a pure equilibrium. Hence both mix with full support. Indifference gives (p,q)=(1/2,3/8) and row value 1/2. At this p both columns yield 1/2, so row guarantees that amount against every column mixture. At this q both rows yield 1/2, so column holds every row mixture to it. These two linear guarantees certify a saddle globally; they are not a local first-order check. Support completeness proves this is the unique Nash equilibrium.

Change only the upper-left row payoff from 3 to 5, retaining the negative column payoff. The two equalities become 6q−1=2−4q and 7p−2=2−3p. The equilibrium becomes (2/5,3/10) with value 4/5. The strict pure-reply cycle remains, so the same completeness argument applies. A more favorable payoff can reduce the probability with which the favored action is used in equilibrium: the opponent’s incentives determine the mixing probability.

The finite proof corresponds to the inspected finite-game scope of Yildiz’s notes, printed pages 36–39. All fixed-point hypotheses were verified above rather than supplied by the citation.

2. Strategic-form perfection: two equivalent definitions

Nash permits some actions to have exactly zero probability. To examine robustness to small mistakes, give each pure action a positive lower probability δi(a)>0, with di=Σaδi(a)<1. The perturbed strategy set is

Xi(δ)={ρi∈Δ(Ai):ρi(a)≥δi(a) for every a}
={δi+(1−di)ri:ri∈Δ(Ai)}.

It is nonempty compact and convex. The strict sum restriction leaves a positive amount of freely allocated probability. For uniform floors ε, require |Ai|ε<1 for every player; arbitrary positive ε need not define a feasible simplex.

Perturbed-equilibrium definition. A profile σ is a strategic-form trembling-hand perfect equilibrium if some sequence δk with every component positive, every player’s sum below one and maxi,aδik(a)→0 admits constrained Nash equilibria ρk→σ. Here each player maximizes on Xi(δk), not on the original simplex.

Existence. For fixed δ, payoffs remain continuous and linear on ∏Xi(δ). The constrained best-reply correspondence is nonempty compact convex and has a closed graph: compare every constrained alternative and pass the continuous payoff inequalities to the limit. Equivalently, compare its finitely many vertices δi+(1−di)ea. Kakutani therefore gives a perturbed equilibrium. With m=maxi|Ai|, choose uniform εk=1/(km+1), k≥1. All simplex sums are below one and the floors vanish. Compactness of the unperturbed product gives a subsequence of equilibria converging to some σ. Hence every finite strategic-form game has a perfect equilibrium.

Every such limit is Nash. For any pure bi, the feasible perturbed deviation δik+(1−dik)ebi converges to ebi. The constrained best-reply inequality against this deviation passes to the limit and yields Ui(σ)≥vi(bi,σ−i). A forbidden unperturbed deviation must first be approximated by a feasible one; it cannot be inserted directly into the perturbed game.

Equivalent tremble-sequence characterization. A profile σ is perfect if and only if there are fully mixed profiles τk→σ such that, for every k and i, the fixed limiting strategy σi is an unconstrained best reply to τ−ik. The τk themselves need not be Nash equilibria of the unperturbed game.

From perturbations to trembles. Suppose ρk→σ are equilibria with vanishing floors. For any a in the support of σi, convergence and positivity give ρik(a)>δik(a) eventually. In a constrained linear optimum, an action with probability strictly above its floor must maximize payoff among all pure actions: otherwise transfer a small amount of this excess probability to a better action, preserving every floor and the probability sum, to improve. There are finitely many players and supported actions, so one common tail works for all of them. On that tail every action supported by σi is best against ρ−ik; their mixture σi is best too. Every ρk is fully mixed. Set τk equal to this tail and reindex.

From trembles to perturbations. Suppose the characterization holds, and let Si be the nonempty support of σi. Define

δik(a)=τik(a) if a∉Si,
δik(a)=min{τik(a)/2,1/k} if a∈Si.

All floors are positive. Their sum is strictly below one because on every supported action they are at most half its positive τ probability, while outside the support they equal that probability. They vanish: outside Si, τik(a)→σi(a)=0; inside, the floor is at most 1/k. The profile τk is feasible. By the support criterion, each action in Si is best against τ−ik. Every action outside Si is played exactly at its required floor, and all freely allocated mass is placed on Si. The formula for Xi(δ) shows this maximizes payoff over the constrained simplex. Thus τk is a perturbed equilibrium for these floors, proving the reverse implication.

Dominance and two sufficient cases. A pure action a is weakly dominated by a mixture ri if ui(ri,a−i)≥ui(a,a−i) for every opponents’ pure profile, with a strict inequality somewhere. Fully mixed opponents give positive probability to every such profile, so ri strictly beats a in expectation. The tremble characterization therefore excludes a from every perfect support. This is a necessary condition, not a general converse.

A strict pure Nash equilibrium is perfect: finitely many strictly positive payoff gaps remain positive for opponents’ profiles sufficiently close to the equilibrium. Mixing each player’s equilibrium action with a vanishing amount of uniform noise gives a fully mixed sequence against which the original pure choices stay best. A fully mixed Nash equilibrium is also perfect: take the constant sequence τk=σ. Neither statement says that all Nash equilibria are perfect or that the refinement selects a unique one.

This section is about the strategic form. It does not assert that perturbing complete contingent plans is the same as perturbing independent decisions at every information set in an extensive game. Manea’s notes, Section 19, printed pages 45–47, motivate the two characterizations and distinguish extensive-form concerns. The equivalence proof omitted there is supplied here, with feasible floors and the common finite tail explicit.

Worked case 2: an equilibrium continuum collapses under trembles

Rows U,D and columns L,R have payoff pairs (((2,2),(1,2)),((2,1),(0,0))). With p=Pr(U), q=Pr(L), row’s U−D payoff difference is 1−q and column’s L−R difference is 1−p. If q<1, row must choose p=1; if p<1, column must choose q=1. Conversely either p=1 or q=1 makes both choices best replies. The complete Nash set is the union of the top and right edges of the probability square: p=1 or q=1.

With the same floor ε on each action, 0<ε<1/2, both p and q are at most 1−ε. Both payoff differences are therefore strictly positive. The unique constrained equilibrium is p=q=1−ε, with each payoff 2−ε−ε². At ε=1/10 this gives probabilities (9/10,9/10) and payoffs (189/100,189/100). Its limit is (U,L).

To establish uniqueness among all perfect limits, not only uniform-floor limits, note that D is weakly dominated by U and R by L. Every perfect equilibrium therefore has p=q=1. This profile is indeed perfect since U and L are best against every fully mixed opposing profile. It is not a strict pure equilibrium—both players are indifferent at (U,L)—so its perfection is justified by that direct sequence argument.

Worked case 3: perfection can preserve all three equilibria

Change the payoff table to (((4,4),(0,2)),((2,0),(3,3))). Row’s U−D difference is 5q−3 and column’s L−R difference is 5p−3. The pure equilibria (U,L) and (D,R) are strict. If one player alone mixed while the other were pure, it would face a strict pure best reply and could not mix. Thus every remaining equilibrium has both players mixing. Indifference gives (3/5,3/5) and expected payoffs (12/5,12/5). These are all the Nash equilibria.

The two pure equilibria are perfect by strictness, and the interior equilibrium is perfect by the fully mixed criterion. All three survive. The payoff pair (4,4) exceeds both (3,3) and (12/5,12/5) coordinatewise, so perfection alone does not select the Pareto-superior outcome. Existence, robustness to the specified trembles and welfare ranking answer different questions.

3. Bayesian games: condition on the type that actually arrived

Let Ti be each player’s finite type set, π a common prior on T=∏Ti, and ui(a,t) the payoff. Assume every own-type marginal πi(ti)>0. Joint type profiles may still have zero probability, and types need not be independent. Player i observes ti and uses a mixed action σi(·|ti). Conditional on the type profile, private randomizations are independent across players. Against opponents’ strategies, the payoff from choosing pure bi is

Vi(bi|ti,σ−i)
=Σt−i[π(ti,t−i)/πi(ti)] Σa−iui(bi,a−i,ti,t−i)∏j≠iσj(aj|tj).

A Bayesian Nash equilibrium (BNE) makes every σi(·|ti) a best reply under these conditional values. The finite support criterion applies type by type. When types are correlated, replacing π(t−i|ti) by unconditional marginals changes the game’s beliefs.

Existence through type-agents. Create one agent (i,ti) for every player/type pair, with action set Ai. Give this agent the conditional expected payoff in the displayed formula. It depends on the chosen actions of the opponents’ realized type-agents; the same player’s other, mutually exclusive type-agents do not affect it. This is a finite strategic-form game. Its mixed extension has exactly the conditional polynomial payoff formula above, so the proved finite Nash theorem gives a profile of typewise mixed actions satisfying all BNE inequalities. Independence of different agents’ randomization causes no extra restriction on the one realized type of a player: only that type’s marginal randomization is used. This proves existence for the stated finite Bayesian model.

Ex ante versus interim. For a fixed player, expected gain from changing the entire type-contingent strategy is Σtiπi(ti) times its conditional gain at that type. Typewise optimality therefore prevents all ex ante gains. Conversely, a strictly profitable conditional deviation at a positive-probability type can be made only at that type, leaving all others unchanged; it produces a strictly positive ex ante gain. Thus ex ante optimality and typewise optimality are equivalent here. Randomizing over complete contingent plans gives the same realized outcomes as their typewise marginals when players draw plans independently of Nature and each other; dependence across one player’s unrealized types is immaterial to this one-shot model.

If πi(ti)=0, the ratio defining the conditional prior is undefined and an ex ante criterion places no weight on that type’s choice. One must omit the type or supply additional conditional beliefs and impose its interim conditions separately. It is incorrect to claim that arbitrary ex ante choices there have thereby been shown conditionally optimal. No infinite-type, measurability or unbounded-expectation theorem is being asserted. The inspected finite type-agent and positivity scope is in Yildiz, printed pages 68–75.

Worked case 4: all five equilibria of a private-cost entry game

Each of two firms independently has cost c∈(1,3), each with probability 1/2. Not entering, N, pays zero. Entering, E, pays (4,4) as the revenue and competition coefficient in 4−c−4·1{the other enters}. Each firm sees only its own cost. Let ℓi and hi be its entry probabilities at low and high cost, and qi=(ℓi+hi)/2 its aggregate entry probability.

Independence makes the opponent’s conditional entry probability equal to q−i at either type. The gains from entry are 3−4q−i for low cost and 1−4q−i for high cost. Hence the complete aggregate best-reply correspondence is

B(q)={1} if q<1/4;
B(1/4)=[1/2,1];
B(q)={1/2} if 1/4<q<3/4;
B(3/4)=[0,1/2];
B(q)={0} if q>3/4.

To solve q₁∈B(q₂), q₂∈B(q₁) completely, partition q₁ by these five regions. If q₁<1/4, then q₂=1 and consistency forces q₁=0; if q₁>3/4, q₂=0 and q₁=1. If q₁ is strictly between the thresholds, q₂=1/2 and then q₁=1/2. At q₁=1/4, q₂ lies in [1/2,1], but the only q₂ whose response contains 1/4 is 3/4. The symmetric boundary gives (3/4,1/4). Thus all aggregate BNE pairs are ((0,1),(1/4,3/4),(1/2,1/2),(3/4,1/4),(1,0)).

The corresponding type strategies at aggregate levels 0,1/4,1/2,3/4,1 are respectively ((0,0),(1/2,0),(1,0),(1,1/2),(1,1)), in the order (low-entry,high-entry). These mappings follow from which type can be indifferent at each opponent’s equilibrium probability; they are not a claim that every aggregate rate identifies type behavior outside equilibrium. Ex ante payoff pairs in the displayed equilibrium order are ((0,2),(0,1),(1/2,1/2),(1,0),(2,0)). For example, at (1/4,3/4), player 1’s low type is indifferent and high type stays out, giving zero. Player 2’s low type earns 2 when entering and high type is indifferent, giving ex ante payoff 1.

Now keep both cost marginals unchanged but replace independence by joint probabilities for (LL,LH,HL,HH) equal to (3/8,1/8,1/8,3/8). If both firms enter only at low cost, the other is low with conditional probabilities (3/4,1/4) given own low and high cost. The respective entry gains are (0,0). Low-only entry is a weak BNE with ex ante payoff (0,0). Substituting the unconditional entry probability 1/2 would incorrectly give gains (1,−1). We have established this changed-prior equilibrium, not enumerated every equilibrium of the changed game.

4. Correlated equilibrium: obedience after a private recommendation

A mediator draws an action profile a from a publicly known joint distribution μ and tells each player only its own recommended action ai. There is no transfer or enforcement mechanism. The player may instead choose another action after seeing its recommendation. A correlated equilibrium (CE) makes obedience optimal under that information. Its finite, unnormalized inequalities are

Ci(ai,bi;μ)=Σa−iμ(ai,a−i)[ui(ai,a−i)−ui(bi,a−i)]≥0
for every i,ai,bi.

If recommendation ai has positive marginal probability, divide by that probability to obtain the conditional expected-payoff comparison. If it has zero probability, every associated term is zero and the inequality is vacuous; no arbitrary conditional distribution is required.

All recommendation-contingent deviations. For a deterministic deviation rule di:Ai→Ai, the ex ante obedience advantage is ΣaiCi(ai,di(ai);μ). Thus the pairwise inequalities prevent every such deviation. Conversely, a rule that changes only one recommendation ai to bi and follows all others has advantage exactly that pairwise term, so requiring all rules implies every inequality. A randomized rule Ki(b|a) gives a nonnegative weighted sum Σa,bKi(b|a)Ci(a,b;μ). Consequently deterministic tests already cover all privately randomized contingent deviations. Opponents continue to obey in each unilateral comparison.

CE distributions form a closed convex subset of the finite probability simplex, because all their constraints are linear. They are therefore compact. They are also nonempty: if σ is Nash, its product distribution μ(a)=∏σj(aj) has

Ci(a,b;μ)=σi(a)[vi(a,σ−i)−vi(b,σ−i)]≥0

by the support criterion. Conversely, a product distribution satisfying CE makes every positively weighted own action a best reply to the same opponents’ distribution, so its marginal profile is Nash. Hence product CE is equivalent to Nash. Convex mixtures of Nash product distributions are CE by linearity. A general CE need not lie in that convex hull, as the next welfare calculation proves. These statements concern the distribution and specified private information; revealing additional information may change obedience incentives.

Worked case 5: a unique best recommendation scheme

Two users choose Y (yield) or A (act). The payoff-pair table, with Y first for each player, is (((6,6),(1,8)),((8,1),(0,0))). We evaluate schemes by the explicitly stipulated sum of these two utility indices in their displayed units; this normative sum is not invariant to arbitrary separate rescaling of the players’ utilities.

The pure equilibria are (Y,A) and (A,Y), each with total payoff 9. Both are strict. Against an opponent choosing A with probability q, Y pays 6−5q and A pays 8−8q. A nonpure equilibrium must have both players mixing, because against a pure action the best reply is strict. Indifference yields Pr(A)=2/3 for each and payoffs (8/3,8/3). These are all Nash equilibria, so every mixture of their distributions has expected total payoff at most 9.

Write μ=(α,β,γ,δ) in order (YY,YA,AY,AA). Row’s Y→A inequality is −2α+β≥0 and A→Y is 2γ−δ≥0. Column’s two inequalities are −2α+γ≥0 and 2β−δ≥0. Along with nonnegativity and α+β+γ+δ=1, these four inequalities characterize the entire CE set. The distribution (1/5,2/5,2/5,0) is CE and gives payoffs (24/5,24/5), total 48/5. Since 48/5>9, it lies outside the convex hull of all Nash distributions.

Global optimality and uniqueness. Welfare is W=12α+9(β+γ)=9+3α−9δ. The first and third obedience inequalities imply β+γ≥4α, hence α≤(1−δ)/5. Therefore

W≤9+3(1−δ)/5−9δ=48/5−48δ/5≤48/5.

Equality requires δ=0, α=1/5 and β+γ=4/5 with β,γ≥2/5. Thus β=γ=2/5, proving the displayed maximizer is unique. This is a global linear bound with an equality certificate, not a search over a probability grid.

When privately told Y, a player assigns probability 1/3 to the other receiving Y and 2/3 to A. Obedience and deviation both pay (8/3,8/3). When privately told A, the other certainly receives Y; obeying pays 8 and deviating 6, the pair (8,6). If the full realized profile is made public, YY tells either player it can gain by acting; this scheme is not obedient under that enlarged information.

Each marginal recommends Y with probability 3/5. Replacing the joint scheme by independent draws with the same marginals produces (9/25,6/25,6/25,4/25). Its row Y→A slack is −12/25, so it is not CE. The payoff table, marginal frequencies and even a desirable average payoff do not identify the necessary information structure.

The recommendation and product-distribution arguments use the finite scope inspected in Yildiz, printed pages 46–48 and 52. Neither a general information-design theorem nor a claim that a public recommendation has the same incentives is being imported.

5. Coarse equilibrium changes when a deviation can be chosen

A coarse correlated equilibrium (CCE) prevents a player from improving by committing to a fixed action bi before observing its recommendation. It requires

Σaμ(a)[ui(a)−ui(bi,a−i)]≥0   for every i,bi.

A fixed randomized deviation is a convex average of these comparisons, so pure fixed actions suffice. The choice to deviate cannot depend on the received recommendation. Summing a CE’s inequalities Ci(ai,bi;μ) over ai yields the CCE inequality. Thus every CE is CCE. The latter also form a nonempty compact convex polytope, but the inclusion can be strict.

If each player has at most two actions, the concepts coincide. For a fixed target b, the term associated with recommendation b is zero. There is at most one other recommendation a, so the CCE inequality is exactly the CE inequality a→b. Repeating for each target and player gives every CE condition. A proposed two-action counterexample to CE versus CCE therefore signals an error about the deviation set.

Worked case 6: three actions make coarse obedience weaker

Actions are 0,1,2. An own action earns 1 if it matches the opponent, 2 if it is one higher modulo 3, and −1 otherwise. The row matrix is ((1,−1,2),(2,1,−1),(−1,2,1)); the column matrix is its transpose, so both players use this same own-versus-other rule.

Choose each diagonal profile (0,0),(1,1),(2,2) with probability 1/3. Following yields each player (1,1). Every fixed deviation faces a uniform opponent and earns (1+2−1)/3=2/3. The joint law is therefore CCE. But seeing recommendation a reveals that the opponent will use a. Deviating to a+1 modulo 3 earns 2 in every case. Each corresponding pairwise CE inequality has slack −1/3. Thus the distribution is not CE.

By contrast, independent uniform play is Nash: every own action earns 2/3 against a uniform opponent. Its product law is therefore CE. The example compares specified distributions and deviation rights; it does not classify every equilibrium of this three-action game or claim that a learning process selects one.

Roughgarden’s Lecture 13, Sections 3.4–3.5, states the conditional versus unconditional distinction for cost-minimization games. We maximize utility here, so the inequalities have the opposite sign. The finite inclusion and two-action coincidence were proved directly above. No learning-convergence theorem follows merely from naming a distribution CCE.

6. Exercises

Use exact fractions. For an assertion about all equilibria, cover all supports or all best-reply regions; a grid is not a completeness proof. Unless otherwise stated, payoffs are the displayed utility numbers, mixtures are independent in Nash calculations, and a CE mediator reveals only each player’s own recommendation.

  1. A changed zero-sum game. Solve case 1 after the upper-left row payoff becomes 5 and the column payoff remains its negative. Prove uniqueness by exhausting support possibilities and give both players’ global saddle guarantees. Explain whether replacing player i’s utility by aiui+bi, with ai>0, changes its best replies; distinguish this from rescaling a social sum.
  2. Complete the finite existence proof. Prove the support-best-reply criterion, equivalence of pure and mixed unilateral deviation tests, and every hypothesis needed to apply the proved C04 Kakutani theorem to the finite mixed-strategy product. Explain why neither a pure equilibrium nor convergence of an adjustment process follows.
  3. Different tremble floors. Derive the complete Nash set of case 2. Give each row action lower bound 1/10 and each column action lower bound 1/5. Find the constrained equilibrium and both expected payoffs. Compare with uniform floor 1/10 and prove uniqueness of the perfect limit among all vanishing positive-floor sequences.
  4. Prove the perfection equivalence. Supply both directions, including a single finite tail for supported actions, positive floors with sum below one and vanishing floors. Explain why the tremble profiles need not be unconstrained Nash equilibria. Illustrate the reverse construction at k=10 with σi=(1/2,1/2,0) and τi=(9/20,9/20,1/10), assuming σi is best against the given opponents’ trembles. Calculate its floors and freely allocated probability vector.
  5. Dominated only by mixing. Row actions T,M,D have respective payoff vectors ((2,0,2),(0,2,2),(1,1,1)) against columns X,Y,Z; every column-player payoff is zero. Show that no single pure row action weakly dominates D, but a mixture does. Prove that row D and column mixture (1/2,1/2,0) form a Nash equilibrium which is not perfect. Generalize the exclusion argument to any pure action weakly dominated by a mixed strategy. Prove the separate claims that strict pure Nash and fully mixed Nash are perfect.
  6. Refinement and selection. Derive all three equilibria of case 3 and establish perfection of each. Then change only the lower-right payoff pair from (3,3) to (5,5). Find all equilibria again, including exact mixed payoffs, and state which survive perfection. What has and has not been selected?
  7. The complete Bayesian entry correspondence. Under case 4’s independent equally likely costs, derive the entire piecewise aggregate best-reply correspondence, prove that exactly the five listed aggregate pairs are BNE, recover each type strategy and compute each ex ante payoff pair. Explain why aggregate entry does not generally identify typewise behavior outside these equilibrium conditions.
  8. The same marginals, different beliefs. Verify the low-only-entry BNE under case 4’s correlated prior. Replace its joint law by (LL,LH,HL,HH)=(1/8,3/8,3/8,1/8), retaining both marginals. Compute conditional entry gains and ex ante payoffs under low-only entry, and check every type’s optimality. Finally suppose an own type has marginal probability zero. Explain exactly what ex ante optimality establishes and what extra specification is needed to demand interim optimality there.
  9. A welfare objective over the CE polytope. Derive all four CE inequalities in case 5, prove the global welfare bound and its unique equality case, and compare with every mixture of Nash distributions. Now change only YY from (6,6) to (5,5). Derive the new CE inequalities and solve the new global sum-payoff maximization, including uniqueness and both individual payoffs.
  10. What exactly does the signal reveal? Prove equivalence of pairwise CE inequalities and all deterministic or privately randomized recommendation-contingent deviations; handle zero-mass recommendations. Prove that a product law is CE exactly when its marginals are Nash and that mixtures of Nash distributions are CE. For case 5’s optimal scheme, compute the private conditional obedience comparisons, diagnose full-profile public disclosure, and test the independent product of the same marginals.
  11. Coarse versus conditional deviation rights. Prove CE implies CCE and prove the converse when every player has at most two actions. In case 6, let μλ=(1−λ)ν+λd for 0≤λ≤1, where ν is the independent uniform product and d is the uniform diagonal law. Derive the payoff from following, each fixed deviation, and the cyclic contingent deviation a↦a+1. Classify CCE and CE throughout this family; report the values at λ=1/2. Do not infer a classification of every equilibrium of the full game.
  12. Referee an equilibrium claim. A report concludes: “Observed action marginals match a mixed equilibrium, so we have identified private beliefs and the unique perfect outcome. We can make all recommendations public without changing incentives. The same unconditional entry rate applies to every cost type. A distribution with no profitable fixed action deviation will be obeyed after recommendations, and repeated best replies must converge because an equilibrium exists.” Write a reasoned correction using specific chapter examples and state what additional evidence or theorem each empirical or dynamic claim would require. Use four dimensions worth three points each: equilibrium/proof; refinement/selection; information/deviation rights; and empirical identification/learning.

7. Complete solutions

Open solutions and scoring guidance

  1. The changed row payoffs against q are 6q−1 and 2−4q, equal only at q=3/10. Against p, columns L and R give row payoffs 7p−2 and 2−3p, equal only at p=2/5. At these probabilities both row actions and both columns yield row value 4/5. Thus every row deviation against q earns at most that value and every column deviation against p leaves row at least that value, giving the global saddle bounds. There is no pure equilibrium: the strict best-reply cycle remains U to L, D to R, R to U and L to D. If one player were pure the other would have a strict pure best reply, forcing a pure equilibrium, which is impossible. Every equilibrium therefore has both players mix, and the unique indifference solution is the unique equilibrium.

    A positive affine transformation multiplies each own expected-payoff difference by ai, preserving its sign and all best replies. Hence it preserves Nash and the incentive inequalities used by perfection and CE. Separate rescaling of different players’ utilities can change which distribution maximizes their sum; a welfare objective must stipulate the relative units rather than infer them from strategic behavior.

  2. Against fixed opponents, the payoff of a mixture is a convex average of finitely many pure-action values. Its maximum is the largest of those values, attained by a pure action. A mixture attains it if and only if every positively weighted action has that largest value. This proves the support criterion and shows that absence of a profitable pure deviation is equivalent to absence of a profitable mixed deviation.

    The product of finite action simplices is nonempty compact convex. For each player the best-reply set is the simplex on its nonempty set of highest-payoff actions, hence nonempty compact convex. If profiles and selected best replies converge, compare each selected reply with every pure alternative; continuity of the finite expected-payoff polynomial passes all comparisons to the limit. The limiting choice is a best reply, so the graph is closed. Products preserve these properties. C04’s proved Kakutani theorem gives a fixed point of the product best-reply correspondence, exactly a mixed Nash equilibrium. The fixed point may put positive mass on several actions; case 1 has no pure equilibrium. No dynamic law or contraction was assumed, so this existence proof establishes no convergence of an adjustment process.

  3. The differences are 1−q and 1−p. If q<1, row must choose p=1; if p<1, column must choose q=1. If either equality holds, the other player’s choice is a best reply, proving the entire Nash set p=1 or q=1. With row floor α=1/10 and column floor β=1/5 on each of their two actions, neither p nor q can equal one. Both differences are strictly positive, so each chooses its largest feasible first-action probability: (9/10,4/5). Row payoff is 2q+p(1−q)=2−β−αβ, and column payoff is 2p+q(1−p)=2−α−αβ, giving (89/50,47/25). Uniform α=β=1/10 gives 189/100 each.

    D is weakly dominated by U, with strict gain whenever the opponent uses R; R is weakly dominated by L, with strict gain whenever the opponent uses D. Full mixing makes both events positive, so no perfect equilibrium can support D or R. Hence every perfect equilibrium is (U,L). This profile is perfect because it is a best reply for each player against arbitrarily small fully mixed trembles. Its uniqueness does not rely solely on following one convenient uniform-floor path.

  4. From constrained equilibria ρk with vanishing floors and limit σ, every supported action of σ eventually has ρ probability strictly above its floor. If such an action paid less than another pure action, transferring a sufficiently small portion of its above-floor mass would be a feasible improvement. Thus all supported actions maximize against ρ−ik. Finitely many players and actions let us choose a common tail on which this holds simultaneously. That tail is fully mixed, converges to σ, and makes every σi a best reply.

    Conversely, from fully mixed τk→σ making σi best, set each outside-support floor equal to its τ probability and each inside-support floor to min(τ probability/2,1/k). Floors are positive; their sum is strictly below one because some positive supported mass is reduced. Outside floors tend to zero and inside floors are bounded by 1/k. In τ all probability above the floors is on support actions of σ, which are best against the opponents’ τ. Linear maximization over the residual simplex therefore makes τ a constrained equilibrium. This proves equivalence. An outside-support action can be suboptimal but still receive forced probability, so τ need not be an unperturbed Nash equilibrium.

    At k=10 the specified τ has inside half-probabilities 9/40, both above 1/10. The constructed floor vector is (1/10,1/10,1/10), whose sum is 3/10. The probability vector above those floors is (7/20,7/20,0), totaling 7/10 and placed only on supported best actions.

  5. Neither T nor M weakly dominates D: T loses at Y and M loses at X. Their half-and-half mixture pays (1,1,2), weakly exceeding D=(1,1,1) everywhere and strictly at Z. Against column mixture (1/2,1/2,0), all three row actions pay 1, so D is a best reply. The column player always receives zero and any column mixture is a best reply. This is Nash. Against any fully mixed column strategy, the dominating mixture’s advantage over D equals the positive probability assigned to Z, so D cannot be a best reply. The Nash profile is not perfect.

    Generally, a mixed strategy weakly dominating a pure action has nonnegative payoff differences against every opponents’ pure profile and at least one strictly positive difference. Fully mixed independent opponents give positive probability to every profile, making the expected difference strictly positive. The tremble characterization excludes the pure action from perfect support. For a strict pure Nash equilibrium, finite strict payoff gaps survive all sufficiently small perturbations by continuity; adding vanishing uniform noise gives the required fully mixed sequence. For a fully mixed Nash equilibrium, the constant sequence at the equilibrium itself suffices. These are sufficient conditions, not converses claiming that absence of weak dominance alone establishes perfection.

  6. Originally the two differences are 5q−3 and 5p−3. The strict pure equilibria are (U,L),(D,R); any other equilibrium must be fully mixed since an opponent’s pure choice gives a strict best reply. Thus p=q=3/5, with each payoff 4(3/5)=12/5. Strict pure and fully mixed Nash profiles are perfect, so all three survive.

    With the lower-right payoff 5, the differences become 7q−5 and 7p−5. The same strict pure equilibria survive, now giving (4,4) and (5,5), and the only mixed equilibrium is (5/7,5/7), giving (20/7,20/7). The same support argument is complete, and all three are perfect. Perfection has imposed the stated tremble robustness; it has selected neither a unique outcome nor the Pareto-best one.

  7. Entry gains at low and high cost are 3−4q and 1−4q. If q<1/4 both are positive, forcing (ℓ,h)=(1,1) and own aggregate 1. At q=1/4 the low type enters and the high type may mix, giving [1/2,1]. Between 1/4 and 3/4 only the low type enters, giving 1/2. At q=3/4 only the low type can mix, giving [0,1/2]. Above 3/4 both stay out, giving zero. These regions and boundary intervals cover the entire probability domain.

    If q₁ is below the lower threshold, q₂=1 and mutual optimality forces q₁=0. If it is above the upper threshold, q₂=0 and q₁=1. In the open middle region q₂=1/2 forces q₁=1/2. At q₁=1/4, the other rate is in [1/2,1], and only q₂=3/4 has 1/4 in its best-reply set. At q₁=3/4 the symmetric argument gives q₂=1/4. Thus exactly the five pairs listed in case 4 remain.

    The type plans at own aggregate rates 0,1/4,1/2,3/4,1 are (0,0),(1/2,0),(1,0),(1,1/2),(1,1). For each player, payoff is [ℓ(3−4qother)+h(1−4qother)]/2. Applying it in equilibrium order gives (0,2),(0,1),(1/2,1/2),(1,0),(2,0). The type maps were inferred using the opponent’s equilibrium rate and the relevant indifferent type. Away from that optimality information, the single average q=(ℓ+h)/2 cannot in general identify both ℓ and h.

  8. Under the positive-correlation law, either own-type marginal is 1/2. Conditional probability of an opposing low type is (3/8)/(1/2)=3/4 when own type is low and (1/8)/(1/2)=1/4 when high. Low-only opposing entry therefore gives gains 3−4(3/4)=0 and 1−4(1/4)=0. Both prescribed actions are best replies, weakly. A player’s expected payoff from entering only when low is (3/8)(−1)+(1/8)(3)=0.

    Under the changed joint law the conditional probabilities reverse to (1/4,3/4). The low and high entry gains are (2,−2), so low-only entry is now strict at both types. Expected payoff is (1/8)(−1)+(3/8)(3)=1 for each player, or (1,1). The marginals and prescribed aggregate entry rates stayed at 1/2; the conditional beliefs and payoffs changed. No complete changed-prior equilibrium enumeration was requested.

    With an own type of marginal zero, an ex ante expected-payoff comparison weights every change at that type by zero. It cannot establish conditional optimality there, and the common prior does not define the conditional ratio. Remove the null type or specify additional beliefs and check the typewise best-reply condition using them. For example, if an absent high-cost type is assigned the extra belief that the opponent surely enters, entering has conditional gain −3 and is not optimal, even though its choice affects no ex ante payoff. The extra belief is a new specification, not a deduction from a zero-probability prior event.

  9. At the original YY payoff, row’s two obedience gains are β−2α and 2γ−δ; column’s are γ−2α and 2β−δ. They must be nonnegative, together with the probability constraints. Welfare W=12α+9(β+γ)=9+3α−9δ. The two lower bounds on β and γ give α≤(1−δ)/5, hence W≤48/5−48δ/5≤48/5. Equality forces δ=0, α=1/5, β=γ=2/5. Its payoffs are (24/5,24/5). The complete Nash set consists of the two strict off-diagonal profiles, total 9, and the symmetric interior profile, total 16/3; every mixture of these has total at most 9. The optimal CE is outside their convex hull.

    Changing YY to (5,5) changes the four gains to β−3α, 3γ−δ, γ−3α and 3β−δ. Thus α≤(1−δ)/7. Welfare becomes W=10α+9(β+γ)=9+α−9δ≤64/7−64δ/7≤64/7. Equality again forces δ=0, then α=1/7 and β=γ=3/7. The unique optimal distribution is (1/7,3/7,3/7,0), with individual payoffs (32/7,32/7) and total 64/7. The equality conditions prove uniqueness globally.

  10. The obedience advantage of any deterministic rule d is ΣaCi(a,d(a);μ), so pairwise inequalities imply every rule comparison. A rule changing only one recommendation isolates the corresponding inequality, proving the converse. A randomized rule is a nonnegative weighted sum of the same pairwise terms, so it adds no requirement. A zero-mass recommendation makes its entire row of terms zero and requires no conditional division.

    For a product law, each pairwise term factors as σi(a)[vi(a,σ−i)−vi(b,σ−i)]. Nash support optimality makes all terms nonnegative. Conversely, CE and a positive own probability make the bracket nonnegative for every b, so every supported action is a best reply and the profile is Nash. Linear inequalities also preserve CE under convex combinations; since every Nash product is CE, every mixture of such distributions is CE. This is a distributional claim under the specified information, not permission to reveal all realized actions.

    Under the optimal case 5 scheme, a Y recommendation gives conditional opposing probabilities (1/3,2/3), so obeying pays 6/3+2/3=8/3 and deviating pays 8/3. An A recommendation reveals an opposing Y, giving 8 from obeying versus 6 from yielding. Public disclosure of YY permits a gain from 6 to 8; the event has positive probability, so full-profile disclosure breaks obedience. Marginals Y=3/5 independently produce (9/25,6/25,6/25,4/25), and the Y→A gain is 6/25−2(9/25)=−12/25. Thus matching marginals neither verifies the joint incentive conditions nor identifies private information.

  11. Sum the CE inequality for every possible recommendation a while fixing deviation target b. The result is precisely the unconditional CCE inequality. If a player has only two actions, the recommendation b term is zero and the only other term is its single pairwise CE inequality toward b. Repeating for both targets and all players proves the converse for games in which every player has at most two actions.

    Both ν and d have uniform opponent marginals. Under ν each own action earns 2/3; under d following earns 1 and the cyclic deviation earns 2. Therefore, for μλ, following earns 2/3+λ/3, every fixed deviation earns 2/3, and the cyclic contingent rule earns 2/3+4λ/3. The first is at least every fixed alternative for all λ∈[0,1], so the entire family is CCE. For λ>0 the contingent rule improves payoff by λ, so it is not CE. At λ=0 the law is the independent uniform Nash product and is CE. At λ=1/2, the three payoffs are (5/6,2/3,4/3); each diagonal-style pairwise cyclic inequality has slack −1/6. This classifies the one-parameter family, not every equilibrium of the game.

  12. A defensible memo first distinguishes the claimed concept and its deviation tests. Nash requires a specified independent profile and best-reply inequalities, not merely some marginal frequencies. Case 5 has identical marginals under a CE joint law and a non-CE independent law, so marginal matching does not identify recommendations or private beliefs. Correct conditional beliefs require a stated type law: the three entry priors have the same marginals but different typewise entry gains. Null own types require additional beliefs or omission.

    Perfection is a robustness refinement with a proved tremble characterization, not a universal selection rule. Case 3 has three perfect equilibria, including Pareto-inferior ones. Full public disclosure of the case 5 profile makes the YY recommendation disobeyed. Coarse equilibrium protects only against unconditional deviations; case 6 has no profitable fixed action deviation but a profitable recommendation-contingent rule. Finally, a fixed-point existence theorem does not state a dynamic adjustment law, let alone prove convergence. A convergence claim requires a precise process, information/timing conditions and a relevant stability or learning theorem.

    For empirical identification the author must specify observables, the joint information structure, utility and type primitives, restrictions separating observationally equivalent models, and an estimation or experimental design. For selection it needs a stated selection mechanism and evidence or a theorem supporting it. The chapter’s finite synthetic cases demonstrate logical distinctions; they do not estimate how agents behave.

    Rubric, 12 points. Score each of the four requested dimensions from 0 to 3. Zero means absent or materially false; 1 notices a concern but gives no valid reason; 2 gives a valid diagnosis without a sufficient repair; 3 gives the valid diagnosis, a specific supporting argument or counterexample, and the additional specification/evidence needed. In the first dimension require the correct equilibrium and support tests; in the second distinguish perfection from unique or efficient selection; in the third distinguish conditional beliefs, private information and deviation rights; in the fourth distinguish logical existence from identified behavior or proven learning. Equivalent reasoned memos can receive full credit.

8. Teach-back, retention and reproducibility

Teach-back. Explain why “nobody wants to deviate” is incomplete without specifying information and the allowed deviation. Use one comparison involving type information and one involving recommendations.

Answer guide. In Bayesian entry, a firm conditions on its own cost and evaluates the other firm’s entry through the joint type law; the same marginal entry rate can imply different conditional incentives. In CE, a player may choose an action after its recommendation arrives, so obedience is tested separately for each recommendation, or equivalently against all contingent rules. In CCE it must choose its fixed deviation before seeing that recommendation. The uniform diagonal three-action law satisfies the latter but fails the former. Give credit for the actual conditional calculation and the timing of the deviation, not just the names of the concepts.

Delayed retention. Reconstruct the mixed Nash support test; explain why supported actions in a perturbed limit need one common finite tail; state the role of positive own-type marginals; and show in one sentence why CE and CCE coincide with at most two actions per player.

Answers. Supported actions must all attain the highest pure-action payoff; linearity then handles every mixture. Finitely many positive limiting support probabilities eventually exceed all their vanishing floors simultaneously, allowing the best-reply argument for every player on one tail. Positive own-type marginals define conditional beliefs and convert a profitable typewise deviation into a positive ex ante gain. With at most two actions, a CCE inequality toward b has a zero term when b was recommended and only one remaining term, exactly the other action’s CE inequality.

Reproduce. Use fractions to reconstruct both zero-sum indifference equations, the tremble payoffs, all five Bayesian entry outcomes and the recommendation inequalities. Editorial checks independently enumerate bounded finite deviation rules and small CE-polytope vertices, reconstruct every printed numerical marker and exercise transfer, and reject malformed probability or game inputs. These finite witnesses support the arithmetic; the chapter supplies the universal existence, equivalence and completeness proofs. No external dataset, calibrated behavior or convergence simulation is used.

9. Source scope and the dynamic bridge

Manea’s Non-Cooperative Games is dated January 19, 2017 on its first page, despite its location in a 2016 MIT course. The inspected scope is pages 1 and 45–47, with actual images of pages 1 and 45. Yildiz’s Graduate Game Theory has a Spring 2022 cover on a 2024 course page; the inspected finite-game, CE and Bayesian sections are printed pages 36–39, 46–48, 52–53 and 68–75, with selected equation images. Roughgarden’s November 4, 2013 Lecture 13 was inspected for the private versus coarse deviation definitions on pages 5–7. The bound source record retains exact versions, physical-page mappings and proof limits. No whole-PDF verification, extensive-form perfection result, learning theorem or universal belief-space theorem is claimed.

Dynamic and repeated games adds histories, information sets, sequential credibility and intertemporal incentives. A strategic-form equilibrium alone does not tell us what happens after an unexpected history. Those additional conditional choices and belief restrictions require their own definitions and proofs.
